title: Russian stones and CZ in fashion jewellery: what you are buying
description: What do Russian stones, CZ, Monalisa and doublet mean on a jewellery listing? A plain guide to lab-made stones and how to judge their quality yourself.
intro: When a fashion jewellery listing says 'Russian stones' or 'CZ', it is describing lab-made stones, not natural gems. CZ means cubic zirconia, a man-made crystal that imitates diamond and coloured gems. 'Russian stone' is a trade name rather than a gem category, and sellers use it for high-shine lab stones, especially rich coloured ones like emerald green and ruby red. Knowing what sits behind these labels helps you compare pieces fairly and pay for quality, not names.

sections.heading: Why 'Russian'?
paragraphs: Cubic zirconia as a commercial stone is commonly traced back to research in the Soviet Union in the 1970s, where methods were developed to grow these crystals in large quantities. That history is one likely reason 'Russian' became attached to high-quality lab stones in the jewellery trade.
Today, the word tells you very little about where a stone was actually made. Treat 'Russian' as a style or quality label used by the seller, and judge the stones by what you can see.

sections.heading: The stones you will meet on listings
paragraphs: Fashion jewellery uses a small family of materials, often mixed in a single piece. Here is what the common names usually mean:
list: CZ or AD (American Diamond): cubic zirconia, available in clear and many colours. Hard, sparkly and consistent.
Russian stones: usually lab-made coloured or high-shine stones, often large drops or ovals in polki-look and heritage sets.
Glass or crystal: cheaper, lighter on sparkle, and softer, so facets can get scratched with time.
Monalisa stones: a popular Indian trade name for soft, semi-transparent coloured stones, often in pastel shades, used in Kundan and fusion pieces.
Doublets: two layers bonded together, for example a coloured base under a clear top, to create depth of colour cheaply.

sections.heading: CZ vs glass: how to tell at home
paragraphs: You do not need equipment for a rough check. Look at the edges of the facets under good light. CZ facets are crisp and sharp, and the stone throws small flashes of rainbow colour. Glass facets often look slightly rounded, and the stone has a flatter, more even glow.

Tilt the piece slowly. Tiny round bubbles inside a stone usually suggest glass. Very uneven colour within one stone, or a visible line where two layers meet, may indicate a doublet. None of these are bad in themselves; they simply explain the price difference between two similar-looking sets.

sections.heading: Judging quality in coloured stones
paragraphs: Coloured stones are where cheap and good pieces look most different. Use these checks, especially on large centre stones and drops:
list: Colour should be even across matching stones. Two 'emeralds' in the same earring pair should not be different greens.
The colour should look rich in daylight, not just under shop lights.
Surfaces should be smooth with no chips, especially on pointed ends of drops.
Settings should hold the stone firmly, with claws or a bezel that does not cover too much of it.
Glued stones should show no shiny glue lines or cloudy patches around the edges.

sections.heading: Where Russian stones and CZ fit in your wardrobe
paragraphs: Large Russian-stone emeralds and rubies give a regal, polki-look necklace its drama, and they photograph beautifully at weddings. Clear CZ and AD suit evening receptions and contemporary bridal looks. Small CZ stones also appear in everyday pieces, such as a pendant on a fine chain, where they add a little sparkle without looking dressy.

If you would like to see these stones in context, Varaha's [Heritage collection](/heritage) includes Russian-stone, polki-look and American Diamond sets, and the [925 silver pendants](/silver) use CZ stones in a lighter, daily-wear format.

sections.heading: Caring for lab-made stones
paragraphs: The stones themselves are fairly tough; the weak points are the metal, the plating and any glue. Avoid soaking, especially for glued stones and doublets, because water can creep between layers and fog them. Clean the surface with a dry, soft brush and a microfiber cloth. Keep pieces separate in storage so harder stones do not scratch softer ones, and remove jewellery before applying perfume or hand cream, since residue is what makes sparkly stones look dull.

faq.a: In fashion jewellery, 'Russian stones' usually means lab-made stones chosen for colour and shine. They are not natural gems.
CZ is harder and sparkles more, so it usually stays crisp for longer. Good glass can still look lovely, especially in Kundan work.
The stone does not change, but dirt and oils on the back make it look dull. A gentle clean brings the sparkle back.
It is a trade name for a lab-made green stone used in fashion jewellery to imitate emerald, not a natural emerald.
